newsitem.title: UK: UK managers sceptical of Labour tax pledges.
newsitem.headline: UK managers sceptical of Labour tax pledges.

text.p: Sixty-three percent of British managers are sceptical about the opposition Labour party's pledge not to increase income tax if it comes to power, according to a poll by the Institute of Management.

"Managers still question the Labour party's credibility on the key issue of tax," it said. The poll of 405 managers showed they also questioned the desirability of the "bidding war" on tax cuts being waged by the two main parties.
"Seventy-four percent believe further cuts in income tax would not be prudent, given the standard of public services in the UK," the institute said.
Labour recently pledged not to increase the income tax rates it would inherit from the Conservatives if it wins the election, which is due by May 22 at the latest.
Support for the ruling Conservatives among managers had dropped to 41 percent from 62 percent at the last election in 1992, while support for Labour had increased to 25 percent from 13 percent.
Fifty-nine percent of managers expected the economy to improve over the next 12 months and fifty-five percent expected their own business to grow.

"But 53 percent do not think they will be better off financially in the coming year and almost a third feel insecure in their current jobs," the institute said. "Job insecurity rises to 52 percent among middle and junior managers."
